tagline: Gentle curves follow an old travel corridor through hills, forests and farmland.
intro: The Natchez Trace Parkway is a two-lane, 444-mile road through Tennessee, Alabama and Mississippi, following gentle curves and low ridges. Forests, wetlands, pastures and croplands vary the corridor. Tennessee’s transportation department identifies its historic, cultural, natural and scenic qualities as the basis for its 1996 National Scenic Byway and All-American Road designations. Commercial traffic is prohibited. Most of the route has a 50-mile-per-hour limit, reduced to 40 north of Leiper’s Fork, Tennessee, and at Ridgeland, Mississippi.

The modern road commemorates an older corridor through Chickasaw and Choctaw lands, used by American Indians, boatmen, settlers, slave traders and soldiers. Congressman T. Jeff Busby proposed the parkway as a tribute to that route. President Franklin Roosevelt ordered a survey in 1934 and signed the legislation creating the parkway in 1938. The final two Mississippi gaps opened in 2005. Segments of the Old Trace itself survive.

From Pasquo at TN 100, the route heads south toward Birdsong Hollow, then crosses northwest Alabama and the Tennessee River at Colbert Ferry. The bridge at Birdsong Hollow closed in April 2026; reopening is expected in early 2027. Farther south, the parkway passes Tupelo and Jackson before reaching Emerald Mound near Natchez and its southern end at Liberty Road.

moments.title: Double Arch Bridge
moments.text: The Double Arch Bridge carries the parkway’s two lanes 145 feet above Tennessee State Route 96 and a wooded valley. Its arches consist of 122 hollow concrete segments precast in nearby Franklin. There are no upright spandrel columns between arches and deck; the weight concentrates at the crowns. During construction, temporary cables supported the arches, avoiding conventional shoring towers to reduce damage to the valley. The bridge opened in 1994 and won a Presidential Award for Design Excellence the following year. The bridge closed in April 2026 for installation of a permanent pedestrian safety barrier.

moments.title: Colbert Ferry
moments.text: At Colbert Ferry, the Tennessee River crossing and a place to spend the night once formed a single stop on the Trace. Chickasaw George Colbert operated the ferry from 1800 to 1819 and kept an inn nearby. Inns along the old route were called stands, offering food and lodging as traffic increased. The inn itself is gone: Alabama Tourism directs visitors to its former site, a 50-yard walk from the parking area. The ferry stop lies on the river’s southern shore. Across the river, Lauderdale offers a view from the northern bank.

moments.title: Emerald Mound
moments.text: Emerald Mound began with a natural hill that workers enlarged by depositing earth along its sides. The resulting platform covers eight acres and rises 35 feet, with two smaller mounds on top. The site belongs to the Plaquemine culture and later served the historic Natchez people as a ceremonial center. Six other secondary mounds were lost to erosion and plowing in the nineteenth century. The National Park Service stabilized Emerald Mound in 1955. Its present name comes from the nineteenth-century Emerald Plantation that surrounded it, rather than from the people who built the earthwork.
moments.notice: Two smaller mounds rise from the flat top of the main earthwork.
